purpose: Five distinct UNESCO World Heritage country gateway drafts: Bulgaria, Marshall Islands, Palestine, Sweden and El Salvador.

sections.title: A monastery in the Rila Mountains
sections.body: Rila Monastery occupies a mountain valley in south-western Bulgaria. Its buildings developed around an Orthodox religious community associated with Saint John of Rila. Forested slopes and the narrow valley form part of the experience of the site. The architecture is important, but the location also helps explain why a religious retreat could become a lasting centre of pilgrimage and cultural life.

sections.title: Walls, courtyards and paintings
sections.body: The monastery contains a large enclosed courtyard, a church and residential buildings. Painted galleries and decorated interiors show traditions of religious art and skilled craftsmanship. Much of the present complex was rebuilt during the nineteenth century after an earlier fire. Calling every visible structure medieval would therefore misrepresent its history and the continuity of the community through change.

sections.title: Cultural and educational roles
sections.body: Monastic institutions could preserve manuscripts, religious knowledge and artistic practices through changing political circumstances. Rila has held significance in Bulgarian culture over many centuries, and this continued during periods when the surrounding region belonged to larger states. The monks, artists and supporters all contributed to that continuity. It is not simply a monument connected with one national historical event.

sections.title: Conservation in a mountain setting
sections.body: Weather, large visitor numbers and maintaining buildings in use create practical challenges. Historic painting and timber need different kinds of care from exposed masonry. The surrounding forest and mountain landscape also require consideration. Rila demonstrates how preserving a living religious site involves architecture, artistic traditions and an environment that has helped shape its purpose.

records.hook: Marshall Islands — Bikini Atoll Nuclear Test Site

sections.title: An atoll with a difficult modern history
sections.body: Bikini Atoll belongs to the Marshall Islands in the central Pacific. Its lagoon, low islands and coral formations are part of an oceanic environment whose recent history was transformed by nuclear testing. UNESCO recognises the atoll as a World Heritage property because of its significance to twentieth-century history. Its inclusion is not a celebration of the tests or their consequences.

sections.title: Displacement and consequences
sections.body: The testing programme took place after the Second World War and required local communities to leave their homes. It also had long-lasting environmental, health and social consequences. The experiences of Bikini's people are essential to any responsible account. Presenting the atoll only as an unusual collection of underwater objects would overlook the disruption to families and their relationships with the land.

sections.title: Evidence in the landscape
sections.body: Physical traces of the testing era remain both on land and below the lagoon. Researchers examine environmental conditions and historic records to understand the site, while recognising that access and restoration present complex problems. Coral-reef ecology and water movement continue around the atoll, but their presence should never be used to suggest that earlier harm has simply disappeared.

sections.title: Memory and heritage responsibility
sections.body: The World Heritage designation asks visitors to reflect on what happened and why the site matters today. Conservation includes documenting events, acknowledging affected communities and caring for an altered island environment. Bikini is a case study of how heritage can preserve evidence of harmful historical decisions, not only achievements in architecture or art.

records.focus: Church of the Nativity and Pilgrimage Route, Bethlehem
records.hook: Palestine — Church of the Nativity and Pilgrimage Route, Bethlehem

sections.title: A historic centre of pilgrimage
sections.body: The Church of the Nativity stands in Bethlehem, a city south of Jerusalem. Christian tradition identifies the place beneath the church with the birth of Jesus, and the site has been a focus of pilgrimage for many centuries. UNESCO's World Heritage property includes the church complex and part of a historic route through the city. Its importance is religious, architectural and urban.

sections.title: Buildings from different periods
sections.body: The church visible today retains substantial early Byzantine fabric, with later additions and restoration. Floor mosaics and religious spaces preserve evidence of how the site was maintained and reinterpreted. Adjacent convents and buildings are used by different Christian communities. The architectural ensemble was not built or administered by one institution at one moment in history.

sections.title: An active part of Bethlehem
sections.body: The pilgrimage route passes through streets that remain connected with daily urban life. Residents, businesses, worshippers and visitors use the surrounding area in different ways. Conservation needs to recognise those activities alongside the care of paintings, stone and older structures. The site belongs to a city with a long and complex history that extends beyond the church itself.

sections.title: Preserving heritage during uncertainty
sections.body: Work on historic places requires expertise, resources and access, which can become difficult during periods of political instability. The heritage should be described with respect for the people who use and maintain it, without confusing a protected cultural property with a claim that resolves wider political questions. Bethlehem offers an example of a living place whose meaning reaches across generations and communities.

sections.title: A coastline still rising
sections.body: Sweden's High Coast lies along the northern Baltic region, where steep shores, hills and inlets reveal a landscape transformed by ice. The protected World Heritage property also includes Finland's Kvarken Archipelago, whose low islands provide a contrasting environment. Both areas preserve evidence of glaciation and subsequent land uplift. Understanding the site requires thinking over thousands of years, not only today's shoreline.

sections.title: Land freed from the weight of ice
sections.body: A great ice sheet pressed down the Earth's crust during earlier glacial periods. As the ice retreated, the crust began rising, a process that still affects coastal geography. Islands, bays and shorelines have changed positions relative to the sea. Scientists measure this movement and study the landforms it leaves behind, rather than treating the coastline as a fixed boundary.

sections.title: Ecology on newly exposed land
sections.body: Vegetation develops on ground that rises above water, while shallow bays can gradually become wetlands. Different stages of this process create habitats with contrasting plants and animals. Human settlements and travel routes have also been influenced by shifting coastlines. The geological change is therefore linked to both ecology and historical land use.

sections.title: A shared heritage property
sections.body: This is a cross-border natural site rather than a purely Swedish landscape. Managing it requires coordination over conservation, tourism and research. A viewpoint across land and sea can reveal why small elevations matter over centuries. High Coast / Kvarken provides an unusually visible example of geological change continuing within the lifetime of communities living nearby.

records.hook: El Salvador — Joya de Cerén Archaeological Site

sections.title: A village preserved by volcanic material
sections.body: Joya de Cerén in El Salvador contains remains of a pre-Hispanic agricultural community buried by a volcanic eruption around the early seventh century. The ash preserved details that seldom survive at other archaeological sites, including traces of houses and daily activities. Unlike an ancient city dominated by palaces, this site provides rare evidence of ordinary rural life and its organisation.

sections.title: Farming and household spaces
sections.body: Excavations reveal buildings and areas associated with domestic work, food production and community activity. Their arrangement helps researchers investigate the routines of the people who lived there. Plant material and other fragile evidence can contribute to understanding cultivation. Archaeologists do not know every aspect of village life, but the preserved context makes careful interpretation possible.

sections.title: Volcanoes as both hazard and archive
sections.body: Volcanic activity transformed the landscape and ended occupation at the settlement, while the resulting deposits protected archaeological information from later disturbance. The site therefore illustrates a complicated relationship between natural processes and the historical record. Geological evidence can help reconstruct the sequence of events, and excavation must account for how layers were deposited.

sections.title: Conserving vulnerable remains
sections.body: Earthen structures and exposed archaeological materials can deteriorate when subjected to weather and uncontrolled visitor movement. Protective shelters, documentation and long-term monitoring are important. Joya de Cerén is useful for studying agriculture, settlement patterns and environmental change in Central America, reminding visitors that the everyday lives of rural communities are an essential part of world history.
